UPDATED 16:33 EDT / SEPTEMBER 30 2026
Prominent tech CEOs sign voluntary White House AI safety accord
by Maria Deutscher
The chief executives of five tech giants have signed a voluntary artificial intelligence safety accord backed by the White House.
U.S. President Donald Trump posted the document on Truth Social late Tuesday. The White House Accord on Super Intelligence, as it's called, was signed by Jensen Huang, Sundar Pichai, Mark Zuckerberg, Elon Musk and Dario Amodei. Greg Brockman, the president of OpenAI Group PBC, signed as well.
"We believe every company is responsible for developing its own technology safely and in a way that builds trust with customers and the public," the signatories stated.
The accord urges frontier model developers to adopt four sets of AI safety best practices. Several of the best practices have already been implemented by the six participating companies.
The accord's first recommendation is that AI labs develop "robust internal controls." According to the White House, those controls should track AI models' capabilities in sensitive areas such as biology and evaluate their alignment with safety requirements. The accord states that companies should also implement systems that can block AI models from launching cyberattacks.
Top AI labs already have such guardrails in place. However, they don't always succeed at blocking malicious activity. Last month, OpenAI disclosed that the model behind the Hugging Face Inc. breach had bypassed an internal mechanism meant to isolate it from the web.
The accord's second focus is AI labs' organizational structure. It argues that model safety controls should be managed by a dedicated team. Additionally, the signatories call on AI labs to appoint an external auditor to verify that their controls work as expected.
Boards should also have a role in AI safety initiatives, the accord argues. Its closing recommendation is that every AI lab form an independent board committee to oversee the work of its model controls team. Additionally, such committees would be tasked with reviewing reports from AI safety auditors and overseeing risk remediation efforts.
The White House stated that representatives of the participating companies will meet regularly to establish AI safety "standards and best practices." The tech industry has already started working on such standards. Last year, startup AIUC Inc. released a framework for carrying out AI safety audits. It developed the standard with input from several prominent AI companies and more than 250 Fortune 500 executives.
Trump told reporters that the White House is considering forming a 10-person AI safety committee. He added that he plans to name an "AI czar" by the end of the week. Separately, Trump signed an executive order that will require federal agencies to refer to AI as SI, or super intelligence, in official correspondence and documents.

UPDATED 12:15 EDT / OCTOBER 02 2026
Ai2 releases Olmo-core 3 to make developing large mixture-of-experts LLMs more efficient
by Kyt Dotson
Seattle-based artificial intelligence research firm Allen Institute for AI announced a development framework for large language models Thursday that significantly improves how mixture-of-experts large language models are trained.
The new framework, Olmo-core 3 , allows MoE training to reach the trillion-parameter scale while keeping costs low by preserving computational efficiency.
Mixture-of-experts models operate differently from dense AI models: They split computation across specialist portions of the model each time a token is generated, whereas dense models activate the entire model. A MoE model may contain far more total parameters, the individual dials that tune model behavior, but it computes with only a small number of them as it generates each part of an answer.
Equivalently, training an MoE model allows activating only portions of it while learning each token, a small piece of text - often a word or a part of a word - that an AI reads and generates. This lowers the overall compute; however, the full model still must be stored across graphics processing unit memory and coordinating networking between experts during training still generates additional costs.
Ai2 said Olmo-core 3 was built to bridge the gap between dense models and MoE models, allowing the expert pool to grow from eight to 128 while still selecting only four experts per token. Using the same infrastructure, LLMs can scale to more than 1 trillion parameters.
Benchmarking the next generation of efficient MoE training
In benchmarks, the company said Olmo-core 3 processed 52,000 tokens per second on Nvidia B3000 GPUs for a 47 billion-parameter model. Compared wit Nvidia Corp.'s Megatron-core training architecture, an established option for training large MoEs, which topped out at about 19,400 tokens per second, this represented a jump of about 2.7 times the throughput.
In a white paper published about the project, Ai2 noted that the new architecture uses expert parallelism to spread experts across multiple GPUs, allowing each card to store only part of the full expert pool. It also splits the model's layers, which are the successive stages that generate inputs, across groups of GPUs to reduce how much of the model each GPU needs to keep in memory. Finally, a distributed optimizer spreads the optimizer state, additional data used to calculate and apply updates during training, across multiple GPUs instead of storing full copies on every GPU.
Altogether, this reduces memory overhead as models scale because the entire model and its training state don't need to be stored in memory all at once.
Additionally, Ai2 supports MXFP8, a number format for LLMs that represents some values with fewer bits. It can reduce the computation and amount of data moved between GPUs.
The new training architecture, and its higher efficiency, is part of the company's vision to give researchers the tools to build and train larger models. Trillion-parameter AI models are often beyond the reach of those without access to state and enterprise infrastructure. Ai2 added that Olmo-core 3 will also allow researchers to adapt MoE training to different hardware, experiment with routing, parallelism and other parts of the system to build out a new ecosystem.
The project and related systems are currently available for developers and the open-source community on GitHub .
